claims.text: The initial almost equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy has an FCC structure.
A conventionally cast FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy exhibits soft ferromagnetism.
A conventionally cast FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy has low coercivity.
Cryo-milling followed by rapid consolidation such as spark plasma sintering can produce a nanocrystalline FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy.
Severe plastic deformation causes significant grain refinement.
Nanocrystallization increases the density of grain boundaries.
Grain boundaries in the nanocrystalline alloy act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning sites.
Increased domain-wall pinning raises the coercive field.
The proposed severe-plastic-deformation powder-metallurgy route will produce greater coercivity than conventional casting.
Traditional casting produces relatively larger grains than the proposed powder-metallurgy route.
The coercivity benefit requires formation of a uniform nanocrystalline structure.
Grain coarsening or uneven phase distribution may prevent the coercivity benefit.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on milling duration and sintering conditions.
A greater-than-10% statistically significant coercivity enhancement over the cast control is the specified success criterion.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that no coercivity benefit is expected if a uniform nanocrystalline structure is not achieved, but the falsification rule treats failure to achieve that structure as falsification of the hypothesis. Failure to implement the stipulated intervention does not directly falsify the proposed grain-boundary-pinning mechanism.
